title: Isaac on Mount Moriah
lead: When no way out is in sight, God is already preparing one, long before we are able to see it.
questions: In what part of your life are you begging for rescue when you should first be asking for eyes to see?
Whom have you lately judged for going through their trial too weakly or for too long, though you have never read the first verse of their story?
Whose call, God’s or someone close to you, have you been slow to answer lately with “Here I am”?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: This is the hardest chapter in Genesis, and we won’t pretend otherwise. But the very first verse tells us more than it seems to: “God tested Abraham.” The narrator gives away the ending right at the start, so the reader knows God does not want Isaac dead. Abraham, though, never read that verse. We read from a safe place. He lived it without knowing how it would end. The people around us are also going through trials whose endings they don’t know. No one lives a chapter well when they haven’t been given its first verse.

In the Hebrew of God’s command to Abraham there is a small particle that can be rendered “please.” The command is softened. Yet God Himself counts the cost: “your son… your only son Isaac, whom you love.” He doesn’t question that love; He honors it. This is, in fact, the first place in the whole Bible where the word “love” appears at all. Love makes its debut in Scripture in the setting of a sacrifice.

They walked for three days. Isaac asks about the lamb because he can’t bring himself to ask the real question. Abraham answers, “God Himself will provide the lamb,” saying more than he understands. And when the knife is already in his hand, a double cry comes from heaven: “Abraham, Abraham!” In the entire Hebrew Bible, God’s messenger calls from heaven in only two stories: yesterday over Hagar, today over Abraham. Rescue comes the same way for the slave woman’s son and for the son of promise, so that no one would think God plays favorites.

And here is the sentence we are reading this chapter for: Abraham “looked up and saw behind him a ram in a thicket, caught by its horns.” The ram didn’t drop from the sky at the last moment. It was already there when Abraham noticed it. Just as with Hagar, the rescue lay outside his field of vision. The ram dies “in place of” the son. This is the first time in the Bible that this phrase appears in connection with a sacrifice. The whole temple, which Solomon would later build on this very Moriah, would rest on those words: “in place of.”

The angel says, “you have not withheld your only son.” Centuries later Paul will write about God in words that echo this sentence: “He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all.” What Abraham was spared, God carried through to the end. From then on, no one can say that God asks of people something He has not given Himself.

Yesterday we read about Hagar, who left her child in the desert to die, and whose eyes God opened to see a well. We mentioned that her story has a twin scene in the Bible. Today we turn to it. Genesis 22 is the hardest text in the whole book and one of the hardest in all of Scripture. We won’t pretend otherwise. But this is where we find the sentence that inspired the title of this series: There is hope, because God prepares the rescue before we are able to see it.

sections.heading: The Reader Knows. Abraham Doesn’t.
paragraphs: The first verse says more than it seems to: “Some time later God tested Abraham.” The narrator gives away the ending in the opening sentence. He does it for two reasons. First, it shows the Creator’s character: from the start the reader knows that God does not want Isaac dead. Second, it changes the way we read the rest. We don’t ask whether Isaac will die, because we know this is a test. We ask whether Abraham will be able to bear it.

The word “test” has its own later history, too. The same Hebrew verb shows up at Sinai, where Moses tells the terrified people: don’t be afraid, God has come to test you. The word that chills us in Genesis 22 is meant to calm them in Exodus. A test in the Bible is not a trap set for a person. It is an invitation to show what God already sees in them.

One more thing needs to be said at the threshold of this story. In that world, sacrificing a firstborn son was not unthinkable. On the wall of one Egyptian temple there is a carving of a besieged Canaanite ruler throwing his own son from the city walls, hoping that after such a gift the god would have to save him. That was the religion of Abraham’s neighbors. This whole story is heading toward a finale in which that logic is overturned once and for all: the God of Abraham stops the knife and provides the ram Himself. Genesis 22 does not bring child sacrifice into religion. This chapter pointedly leads it out.

We come to this story from a safe place. Abraham, though, knows neither the first verse nor the ending. That’s worth remembering beyond this story. The people around us go through trials without knowing how they will end. Watching from the outside, we often think we do know, and that is why it’s so easy to decide that someone is handling their trial too weakly, too loudly, or for too long. No one lives a chapter well when they haven’t been given its first verse.

sections.heading: Take, Please
paragraphs: The command itself is built so that a Hebrew reader heard something almost no translation conveys. After “take” comes a small particle that can be rendered “please.” So the command is softened, but the text does not shrink the cost of what God is asking.

On the contrary, God spells it out: “Take your son… your only son Isaac, whom you love.” Three descriptions, each heavier than the one before. God names Abraham’s love for his son before He asks for him. He doesn’t question that love or tell Abraham to suppress it. He honors it. And there is one more detail in this sentence: it is the first place in the entire Bible where the word “love” appears at all. Love makes its debut in Scripture in a sentence about sacrifice. As if the text wanted to say: you will learn what love really is when you feel what it costs.

This call also has an echo. God’s first call to Abraham was: go to the land I will show you. The last one is: go to one of the mountains I will show you. The same wording, the same construction. The first “go” told him to leave his past behind: his country, his clan, his father’s house. The second tells him to risk his future. With one difference: the first call came with a whole list of promises. The second comes with none.

sections.heading: The Two Walked On Together
paragraphs: God didn’t demand the sacrifice on the spot. He told Abraham to walk for three days. Three days of turning it over in his mind, every step on his own feet. The text gives away Abraham’s state of mind in a small detail: he got up early, saddled the donkey, gathered his servants, took his son, and only then split the wood. A man who is thinking clearly doesn’t pack in that order.

To his servants Abraham says, “The boy and I will go over there to worship, and then we will return to you.” We will return. Plural. You can hear in it a merciful lie, a desperate hope, or a faith that holds two irreconcilable things at once: the command and the promise. The Letter to the Hebrews chooses the third: Abraham reasoned that God could raise even the dead. In a believer, especially in a crisis, all of these layers can live side by side, and the Lord knows how to work with every one of them.

Then comes a conversation that in Hebrew is six words of question and six words of answer. It begins with “my father” and ends with “my son.” Isaac asks about the lamb because he doesn’t want to ask outright what he is really asking. Abraham answers, “God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son.” He doesn’t know how it will happen. He says more than he understands. Before this exchange and after it, the same line appears twice, almost word for word: “the two of them walked on together.” They covered the last stretch in a silence that has been called the most eloquent silence in literature.

Look at Isaac for a moment. The word the text uses for him can mean a boy or a young man, and the chapter itself doesn’t let us pin down his age. But we know he carries the wood for the offering. To this day Jewish tradition does not call this story the sacrifice of Isaac. It calls it the Akedah, the binding of Isaac, highlighting precisely the moment he was bound.

sections.heading: Abraham, Abraham!
paragraphs: The knife is already in his hand when a cry comes from heaven: “Abraham, Abraham!” Doubled, urgent, as if the one calling were afraid he might be too late. And the answer is the same one Abraham gave to God at the beginning and to his son on the way: “Here I am.” Three times in this story someone calls him by name, and three times he responds the same way. His whole faith fits inside that readiness: present to God and present to his child. The same toward heaven and toward the people beside him.

The angel says, “now I know that you fear God.” That doesn’t mean the Creator learned something new; the same expression was used in the Sodom account, and it means: it has been confirmed. For Abraham, this moment must have had one more strange side to it. The whole journey, three full days of carrying the heaviest decision of his life, turned out, in human terms, to be unnecessary. The sacrifice called off, the effort seemingly for nothing. And it is exactly here that faith learns its deepest lesson: in the final reckoning, what counts is not our works for God but God’s works for us.

In the entire Hebrew Bible, God’s messenger calls from heaven in only two stories. Yesterday we heard the first of those calls: over Hagar and her dying boy. Today, the second. Rescue for the slave woman’s son and rescue for the son of promise come in the same way, so that no one would think God plays favorites.

And then comes the sentence we are reading this chapter for: “Then Abraham looked up and saw behind him a ram in a thicket, caught by its horns.” The ram didn’t fall from the sky in the last second. It was already in the thicket when Abraham spotted it. Exactly as with Hagar: the rescue lay outside his field of vision until he noticed it. This series is called “There Is Hope” partly because in both of these stories the rescue shows up before despair does.

Abraham had spoken of a lamb and received a full-grown ram. The answer was bigger than the request and different from it, and so it has remained ever since: fulfillment always surprises us; our faith never quite measures up to God’s answer. And one more word from this verse, the most important word in the entire sacrificial system, appears here for the first time in the Bible in the setting of a sacrifice: “in place of.” The ram dies in place of Isaac. All the later service of the temple rests on those words.

sections.heading: The LORD Sees
paragraphs: Abraham named that place “The LORD Will Provide,” a name that could just as well be rendered “the LORD sees.” Yesterday we heard almost the same words from Hagar, who called God “the God who sees me.” A slave woman and a patriarch, each after their darkest night, come back with the same discovery, as though Scripture wanted to give it to us from two independent sources: God sees, and when He sees, He acts.

The name of the mountain is no accident either. Moriah appears only twice in the whole Bible: here, with Abraham, and with Solomon, who builds the temple on Mount Moriah. On the hill where the ram died in place of the son, every sacrifice for centuries would reenact that morning: an animal instead of a person, a gift instead of payment. And at the close of this scene God does something He does only once in all the history of the patriarchs: He swears by Himself. There is no one greater to swear by, so He puts Himself up as the pledge. From that single oath the Letter to the Hebrews will later make the anchor of Christian hope.

sections.heading: A Mountain with a Longer View
paragraphs: One question remains, the one every reader of this chapter asks: what was it all for? Part of the answer comes only from the other end of the Bible. The angel said, “you have not withheld your only son.” Paul will write about God in words that come remarkably close to that sentence: “He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all.” What Abraham was spared at the last moment, God did at Golgotha. Only this time there was no substitute, because He Himself was the substitute.

On Moriah God let one man carry for three days a burden that He Himself intended to carry all the way. Perhaps so that in all of world history there would be at least one father who understands what happened at Golgotha. From then on, no one can say that God asks of people something He has not given Himself. He asked once, as a test, and held back the hand. He gave for real.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: The ram was in the thicket before Abraham ever saw the top of the mountain. The well was in the desert before Hagar stopped weeping. That is the pattern these two stories leave for anyone who can’t see a way out today: you don’t have to create it or force it. It is often prepared ahead of time, waiting just outside your field of vision. Don’t pray only for rescue. Pray for eyes to see it.
